content: Tissue adhesives have been utilized for many years as an alternative to traditional wound closure methods, such as sutures, staples, and adhesive strips, for the management of simple lacerations. These adhesives offer potential advantages, including ease of application, reduced pain during the procedure, shorter application time, and the elimination of the need for a follow-up visit for removal. While previous studies have compared tissue adhesives to standard wound closure methods to evaluate cosmetic outcomes and other secondary measures, no systematic review had been conducted to provide definitive, generalizable conclusions about their effectiveness. The objective of this review was to evaluate and summarize the best available evidence regarding the effects of tissue adhesives on the healing of traumatic lacerations in both children and adults. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Trials Register, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and the Web of Science, covering studies published up to October 2007. Additional sources included clinical trial registries, reference lists of relevant articles, and direct communication with manufacturers and researchers in the field. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared tissue adhesives with standard wound closure methods or compared different types of tissue adhesives. The focus was on acute, linear, low-tension, traumatic lacerations treated in emergency or primary care settings. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. Study authors were contacted for additional information when necessary. Adverse effects were also documented. The outcomes analyzed included cosmetic results (with subgroups based on age, wound location, and the need for deep sutures), pain, procedure time, ease of use, and complications. These outcomes were analyzed separately for two comparisons: tissue adhesives versus standard wound closure, and one tissue adhesive versus another. Thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria for this review. Eleven of these studies compared tissue adhesives with standard wound closure methods. No significant differences were observed in cosmetic outcomes at any time point, as measured by the Cosmetic Visual Analogue Scale (CVAS) or the Wound Evaluation Score (WES). However, tissue adhesives were associated with significantly lower pain scores (Parent VAS weighted mean difference: -13.4 mm; 95% CI: -20.0 to -6.9) and shorter procedure times (weighted mean difference: -4.7 minutes; 95% CI: -7.2 to -2.1). Only one study reported on ease of use, which favored standard wound closure methods. A small but statistically significant increased risk of wound dehiscence was observed with tissue adhesives compared to standard wound closure (Number Needed to Harm [NNH]: 40; 95% CI: 20 to 1168). Conversely, tissue adhesives were associated with a small but statistically significant reduction in the risk of erythema (NNH: 10; 95% CI: 5 to 239). No significant differences were found between the two groups for other complications. Two studies compared different tissue adhesives. One study evaluated butylcyanoacrylate versus octylcyanoacrylate for pediatric facial lacerations and found no significant differences in cosmetic outcomes, pain, procedure time, or complications. Another study compared two formulations of octylcyanoacrylate with different viscosities to assess the incidence of product migration as a proxy for application-related complications. The high-viscosity formulation demonstrated significantly less migration. In conclusion, tissue adhesives are a viable alternative to standard wound closure methods for the repair of simple traumatic lacerations. They provide the advantages of reduced procedure time and less pain compared to traditional methods. However, there is a small but statistically significant increased risk of wound dehiscence associated with their use.
